{{Short description|Game theory term}}
In two-or-more-player [[sequential game]]s, a '''ply''' is one turn taken by one of the players.  The word is used to clarify what is meant when one might otherwise say "turn".

The word "turn" can be a problem since it means different things in different traditions.  For example, in standard [[chess]] terminology, one ''move'' consists of a turn by each player; therefore a ply in chess is a ''half-move''. Thus, after 20 moves in a chess game, 40 plies have been completed—20 by white and 20 by black.  In the game of [[Go (game)|Go]], by contrast, a ply is the normal unit of counting moves; so for example to say that a game is ''250 moves long'' is to imply 250 plies.

In poker with ''n'' players the word "street" is used for a full betting round consisting of ''n'' plies; each dealt card may sometimes also be called a "street". For instance, in heads up [[Texas hold'em]], a street consists of 2 plies, with possible plays being check/raise/call/fold: the first by the player at the big blind, and the second by the dealer, who posts the small blind; and there are 4 streets: preflop, flop, turn, river (the latter 3 corresponding to [[community cards]]). The terms "half-street" and "half-street game" are sometimes used to describe, respectively, a single bet in a heads up game, and a simplified heads up poker game where only a single player bets.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Chen |first=Bill |url=https://www.pokerbooks.lt/books/en/The_Mathematics_of_Poker.pdf |title=The Mathematics of Poker |last2=Ankenman |first2=Jerrod |date=November 30, 2006 |publisher=ConJelCo LLC |isbn=978-1-886070-25-7 |location= |pages=110}}</ref>

The word "ply" used as a synonym for "layer" goes back to the 15th century.<ref>[http://www.etymonline.com/index.php?term=ply Online Etymology Dictionary, "ply"] (cited 24 April 2011)</ref> [[Arthur Samuel (computer scientist)|Arthur Samuel]] first used the term in its game-theoretic sense in his seminal paper on [[machine learning]] in [[checkers]] in 1959,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Samuel |first=A. L. |date=July 31, 1959 |title=Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5392560 |journal=IBM Journal of Research and Development |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=210–229 |doi=10.1147/rd.33.0210 |issn=0018-8646|url-access=subscription }}</ref> but with a slightly different meaning: the "ply", in Samuel's terminology, is actually the depth of analysis ("Certain expressions were  introduced  which we will find useful.  These are: Ply, defined as  the number of moves ahead, where a ply  of  two  consists of one  proposed move  by the machine and  one anticipated  reply by the opponent"<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Samuel |first=A. L. |date=November 30, 1967 |title=Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers. II—Recent Progress |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/5391906 |journal=IBM Journal of Research and Development |volume=11 |issue=6 |pages=601–617 |doi=10.1147/rd.116.0601 |issn=0018-8646|url-access=subscription }}</ref>).

In computing, the concept of a ply is important because one ply corresponds to one level of the [[game tree]].   The [[Deep Blue (chess computer)|Deep Blue]] [[chess computer]] which defeated [[Garry Kasparov|Kasparov]] in 1997 would typically search to a depth of between six and sixteen plies to a maximum of forty plies in some situations.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0004370201001291 | doi=10.1016/S0004-3702(01)00129-1 | title=Deep Blue | year=2002 | last1=Campbell | first1=Murray | last2=Hoane | first2=A.Joseph | last3=Hsu | first3=Feng-Hsiung | journal=Artificial Intelligence | volume=134 | issue=1–2 | pages=57–83 | s2cid=662187 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>
